summary:
Allwork.space opinion piece critiquing LinkedIn's new "Seems like AI slop" report button, added July 30, 2026 to the three-dot menu on every post, with LinkedIn's chief product officer confirming the flags will be fed into the platform's AI detection models.

The author concedes the underlying problem is real. A Pangram Labs study of roughly one million posts (first reported by 404 Media) found 41% of LinkedIn long-form posts over 250 words are fully AI-generated, the highest share of any major platform, ahead of X, Reddit, Substack and Medium. Pangram's CEO called that a floor, not a ceiling. Originality.ai's July 2026 sample of 5,000 posts found more than four in five read as likely AI, and about a quarter of LinkedIn replies now trip AI detectors versus under 2% on Reddit. LinkedIn says it has blocked billions of automated comment attempts recently and is retiring its own AI writing tools.

The core argument: crowdsourced flags are votes, not evidence. A report button captures a feeling, not proof, so flags will encode workplace grudges, competitive sabotage, political dislike, and the general inability of most people to distinguish AI text from clean human prose. The piece uses a fictional founder, Marta, a non-native English speaker whose careful, formal writing reads as machine-made.

Supporting evidence for bias: a 2023 Stanford study ran 91 essays by non-native English speakers through seven AI detectors, which flagged 61% of that human writing as AI, versus roughly 5% false positives for native speakers. The author also notes an engagement paradox: Originality.ai found AI posts earn 45% less engagement on average, but AI "leadership and inspiration" posts outperformed human ones by 75%, implying the most-rewarded slop may be the least-flagged. If a model trains on human suspicion it learns to detect suspicion, a dynamic the author dubs the "Slop Spiral." Text is truncated mid-sentence.
